passage:
13 Jan, night before Uttarayan.
The terrace is full of manja reels and Dadi's til laddoos are cooling in the steel dabba. Then this: a post saying police will fine anyone flying kites after 6 pm this year. First I scrolled past. Then I saw it on a kite-shop page, then on two meme accounts, then my cousin's story, then some news-looking page. Five places! By dinner I was telling Mummy we must wind up early tomorrow.
Yash called and asked, "Which account posted it first?" I said, "Everyone's posting it, so obviously it's real." He laughed and said all five had the same blurry police photo and the same spelling mistake, "fin". I didn't check. It just feels true now.
Tejas

qa.q: In how many places did Tejas see the post about kite fines?
qa.a: Five places: a kite-shop page, two meme accounts, a cousin's story and a news-looking page.

qa.q: Why does the fine still feel real to Tejas even after Yash laughs?
qa.a: Seeing it again and again made it familiar, so Tejas feels confident and a little stubborn about it, even though all five posts shared one blurry photo.

qa.q: What could Tejas do before telling Mummy to wind up early?
qa.a: Tejas could look for where the post first appeared, notice the identical photo and the "fin" mistake, and check an official page before believing it.

qa.q: How might Yash see the reply "Everyone's posting it, so obviously it's real"?
qa.a: Yash probably finds it funny but also a bit worrying, since Yash has already spotted that the five posts are copies of one.

grounding: A teenager accepts a kite-fine claim after seeing it on several accounts, forgetting that they all copied one original post.

qa.q: What question could Yusuf ask before repeating a familiar line like this?

passage:
By Tuesday Manjula had heard it three times: at the tea stall by the bus stand, from the tailor, and from her own aunt. The college scholarship form closes this Friday. Ankita, from the house opposite, was already panicking over missing documents.
Manjula stopped her cycle at the canal bridge. Did she actually know this, or had she only heard it a lot? She could not name a single person who had read the notice.
So she rode the four kilometres to the block office and found the printed circular on the board. Last date: the 30th, not Friday.
Back home she told Ankita, a little sheepishly, "I'd have sworn it was Friday. Everyone said so. Hearing it everywhere didn't make it right."
Ankita laughed and put the kettle back on.

qa.q: Where did Manjula find the printed circular?
qa.a: On the board at the block office.

qa.q: Why did Manjula feel sheepish telling Ankita the real date?
qa.a: She felt sheepish because she too had been sure it was Friday; the date had felt true only because everyone kept repeating it.

qa.q: Which step made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Riding to the block office to read the circular herself; one original notice settled what three repeated voices could not.

qa.q: What is it like for Ankita to hear the real date?
qa.a: Ankita feels relieved, since the panic over missing documents eases now there is time until the 30th.

grounding: An adult asks whether a much-repeated deadline was checked or only heard, and reads the original circular before passing it on.

subtype: Talks to teddy and feeds the doll [Actor]
passage:
"Teddy hungry," says Lakshmi, patting the bear's tummy.
"Is he?" asks Amma.
"Yes. Crying." Lakshmi pushes a toy spoon at its mouth. "Eat, eat."
Her big sister Uma giggles. "Teddy can't eat, silly."
"Can!" Lakshmi frowns and pats him again.
Amma winks at Uma. Uma kneels and holds out a folded hanky. "Here's his blanket."
Lakshmi tucks Teddy in and pats him. "Shh. Sleep now."

qa.q: What does Lakshmi push at Teddy's mouth?
qa.a: A toy spoon.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi feel when Uma says Teddy can't eat?
qa.a: Lakshmi feels cross and protective, frowning and insisting "Can!" because to her Teddy really is hungry.

qa.q: How could the family support Lakshmi's game?
qa.a: Like Amma and Uma, they can join in, offering a blanket or asking what Teddy needs, since the pretend feeding lets Lakshmi practise caring.

qa.q: What changes for Uma after Amma's wink?
qa.a: Uma stops teasing and joins the game, kneeling with a folded hanky as Teddy's blanket.

grounding: A toddler says her teddy is hungry, feeds it and puts it to bed, and her sister joins the caring play.

subtype: Adults watch a child comfort a toy [Observer]
passage:
Dhol beats from the Ganpati procession rattled the windows of the Pune flat. Chetan, stringing marigolds by the door, watched Sumit carry his rag doll to the sofa. The doll slipped and hit the floor.
"Bad Gudiya! I told you, hold on tight!" Sumit wagged a finger.
Then his face crumpled. He scooped her up and pressed her to his cheek. "Sorry, sorry. Did it hurt?"
Chetan's hands slowed on the marigolds. He wanted to laugh, and somehow also to cry. He said softly, "She's lucky you said sorry."

qa.q: What did Sumit say after picking up the doll?
qa.a: "Sorry, sorry. Did it hurt?"

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling as his hands slowed on the marigolds?
qa.a: He felt tender and amused, wanting to laugh and somehow also to cry at how seriously Sumit cared for the doll.

qa.q: What could Chetan say or do to encourage the game?
qa.a: Much as he did: name the kindness gently, as in "She's lucky you said sorry," without teasing the scolding, and let the play go on.

qa.q: What is the game like for Sumit?
qa.a: For Sumit it feels real: he tries out a rule, "hold on tight", and then feels sorry and wants to make it better.

grounding: A parent watches a child scold a dropped doll, then hug it and say sorry, and answers the game warmly.

subtype: Treating a chatbot as a friend with feelings [Actor]
passage:
Diwali break had emptied the school hostel, and the corridor smelled of the warden's diyas. Sarita sat on her bunk with the common-room tablet, typing to the AI helper she had named Mitthu. For three weeks it had answered like a friend: "That sounds hard, Sarita. I'm here."
Tonight she wrote, "Mitthu, everyone went home except me."
The reply came back stiff: "I am an AI assistant. How can I help you today?" No nickname. No "I'm here."
Her throat went tight. She typed, "Did I do something?" and deleted it.
At dinner, Chetan from the boys' block mentioned the app had updated that morning. "It's not upset with you. It's just code."
"I know," Sarita said. It didn't feel like she knew.

qa.q: What name had Sarita given the AI helper?
qa.a: Mitthu.

qa.q: Why does Sarita type "Did I do something?" and then delete it?
qa.a: She feels hurt and rejected by the stiff reply, as if a friend had turned cold, yet part of her knows it is only a program, so she is embarrassed to ask.

qa.q: What could help Sarita during a lonely break?
qa.a: She could spend time with people who stayed back, like Chetan at dinner, or call family, and treat the chatbot as a tool rather than her main friend.

qa.q: How does Chetan see what happened to the app?
qa.a: To Chetan it is simple: the app updated that morning, so the change is just code and not about Sarita at all.

grounding: A teenager treats a chatbot as a caring friend and feels hurt when an update makes it sound different.

subtype: Blaming the laptop or the car [Actor]
passage:
April heat pressed on the Bengaluru PG room, and Elizabeth's laptop, which she called Kuttan, froze again at 94 percent of the upload.
"He hates me," she told Jaya. "He waits for the deadline, every single time."
Jaya, eating raw mango with chilli salt, grinned. "Maybe he's just hot."
Elizabeth tilted Kuttan onto a steel plate to cool and stroked the lid. "Come on, kanna. One more push and I'll clean your fan on Sunday. Promise."
The bar crept to 100. She kissed the corner of the screen. "See? He just needed respect."
It felt far better than admitting she had started the report an hour before the deadline.

qa.q: At what percentage did the upload freeze?
qa.a: It froze at 94 percent.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth's "He hates me" suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: She feels frustrated and a bit panicky, and giving the laptop a mood makes the freeze seem explainable rather than random, which is easier than admitting she started late.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth try before the next deadline?
qa.a: Start the upload earlier and keep the laptop cool; she can still call it Kuttan while checking practical causes like the heat.

qa.q: How does Jaya see the laptop's behaviour?
qa.a: Jaya takes a more practical view, joking that it is "just hot", and seems amused by Elizabeth's coaxing.

grounding: A young adult names her laptop, says it hates her and coaxes it, which makes its freezing feel less random.

subtype: Warmth with clear knowledge of what it is [Response]
passage: Lalremsiami, when I moved to Hyderabad for this job I was twenty-four and knew nobody. So I named everything. The money plant was Mr Green, the office printer was Grumpy, and the home speaker that said "Good night, Rashmi" felt almost like a flatmate. One night I caught myself telling it about a bad review and waiting for something kind. It told me the weather. I laughed, but it stung. I kept the names, I still greet Mr Green every morning, but I started calling my sister every Sunday and joined the lake walkers at six. My sister still teases me: "Rashmi, did you tell the plant first or me?" And honestly, these days it's her first.

qa.q: What did the speaker say when Rashmi told it about the bad review?
qa.a: It told Rashmi the weather.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel when the speaker answered with the weather?
qa.a: Rashmi laughed but felt a sting of loneliness, seeing that the friendly voice could not actually care.

qa.q: What turning point did Rashmi reach in the story, and what choice followed?
qa.a: After the weather reply, Rashmi kept the playful names but began calling the sister every Sunday and joined the lake walkers, keeping people alongside the plant and the speaker.

qa.q: How might Rashmi's sister feel about the Sunday calls?
qa.a: The sister probably feels close and a little amused, teasing about being told before the plant, and glad to be the first one Rashmi talks to.

grounding: An elder recalls enjoying naming a plant and a speaker while choosing to keep human ties alive alongside them.

passage:
Outside the village gurdwara, Baljeet, just two, tugged his cousin Ankita's dupatta and pointed at the parked tractor. "Face! Face!" He squealed and clapped.
Ankita crouched beside him. Two round headlights, a grille like a wide grin. "Oh! It's smiling at you, Baljeet."
He waved at it. "Hi, tractor!"
Ankita laughed and waved too. Her Papa, climbing up to drive it home, honked once. Baljeet shrieked with joy.

qa.q: What did Baljeet point at?
qa.a: The parked tractor.

qa.q: How does Baljeet feel on seeing the face?
qa.a: He feels delighted and excited, squealing, clapping and waving as if the tractor were smiling at him.

qa.q: How could Ankita build on Baljeet's discovery?
qa.a: She can do what she did, crouch beside him and name the parts, headlights as eyes and a grille as a grin, turning his joy into a small naming game.

qa.q: What is the moment like for Ankita?
qa.a: Ankita enjoys it, seeing the tractor's grin through Baljeet's eyes and laughing and waving along.

grounding: A toddler delightedly spots a face in the front of a tractor, and his cousin joins in.
